title: Fast and Faithful: Principled Conditional Flow Matching for Inverse Problems

paper.title: Fast and Faithful: Principled Conditional Flow Matching for Inverse Problems
paper.abstract:
Abstract Flow matching approaches to imaging inverse problems commonly incorporate measurements in two ways. Conditioning-based approaches supply measurement-derived information as a network input, often through concatenation, while inference-guided approaches combine an unconditional velocity field with a separate data-consistency update. In these common formulations, the forward model is not explicitly enforced within the learned conditional velocity field.
We propose a principled parametrization of the measurement-conditional velocity field to solve inverse problems. Under linear interpolation, we express the conditional velocity 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t , 𝒚 ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,{\bm{y}}) in terms of the posterior mean 𝔼 [ 𝒙 1 | 𝒙 t , 𝒚 ] \mathbb{E}[{\bm{x}}_{1}|{\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}] , and characterize that mean as the unique minimizer of a variational objective whose data-consistency term is explicit. We further prove that the velocity field defines a probability flow from the source distribution to the measurement-conditioned posterior. Splitting the variational objective yields a conditional velocity parameterization with operator-dependent data-consistency updates, which we train end-to-end under the flow-matching objective, with no additional guidance at inference.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art PSNR with 50 × 50\times fewer function evaluations than the strongest flow baseline. Varying the sampling steps provides test-time control over the distortion–perception trade-off without retraining.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Imaging inverse problems aim to recover an unknown image from degraded measurements. They arise in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), microscopy, astronomical imaging, and remote sensing [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Because the forward operator is often underdetermined, the measurements do not uniquely determine the image. Reconstruction therefore requires prior information. A common classical approach combines a data-fidelity term with a hand-designed regularizer, such as sparsity or smoothness [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Learning-based methods often replace or complement hand-designed regularization with priors learned from data. Score-based diffusion models [ 8 , 9 ] and flow-matching models [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] provide expressive learned priors for imaging inverse problems [ 13 ] . A key distinction among generative inverse-problem solvers is how and when measurement information enters the reconstruction. A common paradigm uses a pretrained generative model of the image distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) p({\bm{x}}) and introduces measurements during inference. DiffPIR [ 14 ] and DDRM [ 15 ] incorporate data consistency through proximal or spectral updates, while variational PnP diffusion [ 16 ] alternates denoising with data-consistency projections. Flow matching approaches similarly combine an unconditional velocity field with gradient- or projection-based consistency updates [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Inference-time conditioning allows a pretrained prior to be reused across inverse problems and measurement operators. However, the generative dynamics themselves remain unconditional, and measurement consistency is imposed during sampling rather than learned. See Appendix C for further discussion. A second approach trains a score or velocity field conditioned on the measurement 𝒚 {\bm{y}} [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] , removing the need for a separate measurement correction at inference. Here, the measurement enters as a network input–through 𝒚 {\bm{y}} , 𝑨 𝖳 ​ 𝒚 {\bm{A}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}} or a learned embedding–but the forward operator is not applied within the learned dynamics. Operator information is available only through that input and through the paired training distribution. We instead learn a measurement-conditional velocity field that incorporates the forward operator directly into the generative dynamics. Under linear interpolation, 𝒙 t {\bm{x}}_{t} and 𝒚 {\bm{y}} are conditionally independent noisy observations of the clean image 𝒙 1 {\bm{x}}_{1} . Their joint posterior mean determines the optimal conditional velocity, 𝒗 ( 𝒙 t , t , 𝒚 ) = ( 𝔼 [ 𝒙 1 | 𝒙 t , 𝒚 ] − 𝒙 t ) / ( 1 − t ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,{\bm{y}})=\big(\mathbb{E}[{\bm{x}}_{1}|{\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}]-{\bm{x}}_{t}\big)/(1-t) . We show that the posterior mean minimizes a variational objective combining flow consistency, explicit measurement consistency, and implicit regularization. We further prove that the optimal velocity defines a probability flow from the source distribution to the measurement-conditioned posterior. The theoretical characterization makes data consistency part of the conditional dynamics rather than an external sampling correction. The implicit regularizer is unavailable in closed form. We therefore estimate the posterior mean by alternating an operator-dependent data-consistency solve with a learned prior update. The alternating estimator parameterizes the conditional velocity and is trained end-to-end with the flow-matching objective. The forward operator consequently acts within every velocity evaluation rather than entering only as a network input. Our contributions are threefold. (a) We introduce a new flow matching method for imaging inverse problems. Our method provides a systematic way to incorporate the forward operator within the learned measurement-conditional velocity field. (b) We provide a novel theoretical characterization showing that our variational formulation yields the optimal measurement-conditional velocity. We further prove that the associated probability flow transports the source distribution to the measurement-conditioned posterior. (c) Our method achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction using 50 × 50\times fewer function evaluations than the best-performing flow baseline. Our method enables control over distortion–perception trade-off at test time without retraining.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced measurement-conditional flow matching, which embeds the forward operator directly into a learned conditional velocity field. We expressed the optimal velocity in terms of a measurement-conditioned posterior mean and showed that the ideal field transports the source distribution to the corresponding posterior. Across five restoration tasks on two datasets, our method achieves best overall distortion metrics at a fraction of the inference cost of flow-based solvers. Varying the number of sampling steps also allows a single trained model to span the distortion–perception trade-off without retraining. Limitations. Our theoretical analysis assumes a known linear forward model with additive Gaussian noise. Extending the framework to nonlinear measurement processes and more general noise models is an important direction for future work. We also focus on linear interpolation and explicit Euler sampling; investigating alternative probability paths and numerical solvers may further improve sampling efficiency. Finally, our experiments concentrate on two-dimensional image restoration, and applications to other imaging modalities remain to be explored.

sections.text: The proof follows the same two-stage construction as the method. First, we reduce the joint observation ( 𝒙 t , 𝒚 ) ({\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}) to an equivalent Gaussian denoising problem. The Gaussian MMSE characterization of [ 33 ] then gives the variational form of the posterior mean. Second, we show that this mean determines the conditional velocity, that the velocity satisfies the conditional continuity equation, and that its ODE transports the Gaussian source toward the posterior. The lemmas below verify these steps separately, and the final proof combines them.

sections.heading: Appendix C Related Works
sections.text: Generative solvers for imaging inverse problems differ mainly in whether the forward operator 𝑨 {\bm{A}} enters only at inference, through an operator-aware architecture, or during conditional training. We organise prior work along this axis.

sections.heading: Inference-time guidance with a pretrained prior.
sections.text: Diffusion-based methods combine an unconditional prior with measurement consistency at sampling time. DPS and Π \Pi GDM approximate likelihood guidance using denoised clean-image estimates [ 42 , 43 ] ; DDRM and DDNM exploit the spectral or null-space structure of 𝑨 \bm{A} [ 15 , 44 ] ; and DiffPIR, variational PnP diffusion, and DAPS alternate generative updates with optimization, projection, or conditional resampling [ 14 , 16 , 45 ] . Flow-based counterparts include OT-ODE, D-Flow, Flow Priors, FlowDPS, PnP-Flow, and Flower [ 39 , 40 , 19 , 46 , 17 , 18 ] . These methods can reuse a pretrained prior across many compatible operators, but construct only an approximation to the measurement-conditional dynamics at inference. A recent posterior-transport analysis places several such approximations in a common framework and bounds their posterior bias [ 47 ] .

sections.heading: Amortised conditional models.
sections.text: Conditional restoration methods instead learn the measurement-to-image dynamics from paired data. Examples include SR3, Palette, InDI, I 2 SB, conditional diffusion bridges, ResShift, and ResFlow [ 20 , 48 , 21 , 22 , 49 , 50 , 51 ] . Within flow matching, data-dependent stochastic interpolants and conditional Wasserstein formulations provide theoretical foundations [ 52 , 53 ] , while DAWN-FM conditions its velocity field on a measurement embedding, typically 𝑨 ⊤ ​ 𝒚 {\bm{A}}^{\top}{\bm{y}} , and the noise level [ 54 ] . Most such models are trained for a particular task or degradation family and encode the measurement through 𝒚 {\bm{y}} , 𝑨 ⊤ ​ 𝒚 {\bm{A}}^{\top}{\bm{y}} , or a learned representation. Our distinction is that 𝑨 \bm{A} acts explicitly through data-consistency updates inside the generative dynamics.

sections.heading: Operator-aware learned solvers.
sections.text: Plug-and-play methods retain the forward operator in a data-fidelity update while replacing the regularizer with a learned denoiser [ 26 , 37 , 36 ] . Algorithm unrolling makes these iterations end-to-end trainable, yielding methods such as ISTA-Net, ADMM-Net, learned primal–dual, MoDL, and VarNet [ 38 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 ] . MoDL is particularly close in its alternation between data consistency and a shared-weight learned update. These architectures are typically trained as point estimators and do not by themselves define posterior samplers. Our method imports their operator-aware structure into a generative velocity field by applying data consistency at every inner iteration of every ODE step.

sections.heading: Distortion–perception control.
sections.text: The distortion–perception trade-off is fundamental in image restoration [ 59 ] . For MSE distortion and Wasserstein perception, optimal estimators trace a Wasserstein geodesic between the minimum-MSE and perfect-perception endpoints [ 60 ] . PMRF operationalises this idea by transporting a posterior-mean estimate toward the data distribution [ 61 ] ; related interpolation mechanisms appear in InDI and data-dependent interpolants [ 21 , 52 ] . Flow-map denoisers similarly produce a one-parameter family of estimators that traverses the distortion–perception plane, with optimality established in the Gaussian setting [ 62 ] . Our Euler step count N N plays an analogous empirical role. Under the ideal conditional velocity, one Euler step reduces to a conditional-mean update; for a learned velocity field, the N = 1 N{=}1 output should be interpreted as posterior-mean-like rather than exactly equal to the posterior mean. Increasing N N evaluates the learned estimator at progressively lower interpolation noise levels, where posterior modes become more resolvable. Our model is trained for a specified family of forward operators and noise levels, placing it in the amortised conditional family. The central question is whether, given operator-specific training, explicitly embedding 𝑨 \bm{A} in the dynamics improves upon conditioning a network only on an image-space measurement. We investigate this question in Appendix E.2 . We also compare with inference-time flow solvers because they are established reference points for the benchmark [ 39 , 40 , 19 , 17 , 18 ] . Methods that amortise across families of operators [ 63 , 64 ] provide a natural direction for extending our approach.

Kamilov Affiliation: UW-Madison Email: kamilov@wisc.edu Abstract Flow matching approaches to imaging inverse problems commonly incorporate measurements in two ways. Conditioning-based approaches supply measurement-derived information as a network input, often through concatenation, while inference-guided approaches combine an unconditional velocity field with a separate data-consistency update. In these common formulations, the forward model is not explicitly enforced within the learned conditional velocity field. We propose a principled parametrization of the measurement-conditional velocity field to solve inverse problems. Under linear interpolation, we express the conditional velocity 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t , 𝒚 ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,{\bm{y}}) in terms of the posterior mean 𝔼 [ 𝒙 1 | 𝒙 t , 𝒚 ] \mathbb{E}[{\bm{x}}_{1}|{\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}] , and characterize that mean as the unique minimizer of a variational objective whose data-consistency term is explicit. We further prove that the velocity field defines a probability flow from the source distribution to the measurement-conditioned posterior. Splitting the variational objective yields a conditional velocity parameterization with operator-dependent data-consistency updates, which we train end-to-end under the flow-matching objective, with no additional guidance at inference. Our method achieves state-of-the-art PSNR with 50 × 50\times fewer function evaluations than the strongest flow baseline. Varying the sampling steps provides test-time control over the distortion–perception trade-off without retraining. 1 Introduction Imaging inverse problems aim to recover an unknown image from degraded measurements. They arise in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), microscopy, astronomical imaging, and remote sensing [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Because the forward operator is often underdetermined, the measurements do not uniquely determine the image. Reconstruction therefore requires prior information. A common classical approach combines a data-fidelity term with a hand-designed regularizer, such as sparsity or smoothness [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Learning-based methods often replace or complement hand-designed regularization with priors learned from data. Score-based diffusion models [ 8 , 9 ] and flow-matching models [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] provide expressive learned priors for imaging inverse problems [ 13 ] . A key distinction among generative inverse-problem solvers is how and when measurement information enters the reconstruction. A common paradigm uses a pretrained generative model of the image distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) p({\bm{x}}) and introduces measurements during inference. DiffPIR [ 14 ] and DDRM [ 15 ] incorporate data consistency through proximal or spectral updates, while variational PnP diffusion [ 16 ] alternates denoising with data-consistency projections. Flow matching approaches similarly combine an unconditional velocity field with gradient- or projection-based consistency updates [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Inference-time conditioning allows a pretrained prior to be reused across inverse problems and measurement operators. However, the generative dynamics themselves remain unconditional, and measurement consistency is imposed during sampling rather than learned. See Appendix C for further discussion. A second approach trains a score or velocity field conditioned on the measurement 𝒚 {\bm{y}} [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] , removing the need for a separate measurement correction at inference. Here, the measurement enters as a network input–through 𝒚 {\bm{y}} , 𝑨 𝖳 ​ 𝒚 {\bm{A}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}} or a learned embedding–but the forward operator is not applied within the learned dynamics. Operator information is available only through that input and through the paired training distribution. We instead learn a measurement-conditional velocity field that incorporates the forward operator directly into the generative dynamics. Under linear interpolation, 𝒙 t {\bm{x}}_{t} and 𝒚 {\bm{y}} are conditionally independent noisy observations of the clean image 𝒙 1 {\bm{x}}_{1} . Their joint posterior mean determines the optimal conditional velocity, 𝒗 ( 𝒙 t , t , 𝒚 ) = ( 𝔼 [ 𝒙 1 | 𝒙 t , 𝒚 ] − 𝒙 t ) / ( 1 − t ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,{\bm{y}})=\big(\mathbb{E}[{\bm{x}}_{1}|{\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}]-{\bm{x}}_{t}\big)/(1-t) . We show that the posterior mean minimizes a variational objective combining flow consistency, explicit measurement consistency, and implicit regularization. We further prove that the optimal velocity defines a probability flow from the source distribution to the measurement-conditioned posterior. The theoretical characterization makes data consistency part of the conditional dynamics rather than an external sampling correction. The implicit regularizer is unavailable in closed form. We therefore estimate the posterior mean by alternating an operator-dependent data-consistency solve with a learned prior update. The alternating estimator parameterizes the conditional velocity and is trained end-to-end with the flow-matching objective. The forward operator consequently acts within every velocity evaluation rather than entering only as a network input. Our contributions are threefold. (a) We introduce a new flow matching method for imaging inverse problems. Our method provides a systematic way to incorporate the forward operator within the learned measurement-conditional velocity field. (b) We provide a novel theoretical characterization showing that our variational formulation yields the optimal measurement-conditional velocity. We further prove that the associated probability flow transports the source distribution to the measurement-conditioned posterior. (c) Our method achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction using 50 × 50\times fewer function evaluations than the best-performing flow baseline. Our method enables control over distortion–perception trade-off at test time without retraining. 2 Background Inverse problems. Appendix E.4 extends the evaluation to subsampled Fourier measurements, while Appendix E.3 studies posterior sampling and conditional-mean estimation on a toy problem. 5 Conclusion We introduced measurement-conditional flow matching, which embeds the forward operator directly into a learned conditional velocity field. We expressed the optimal velocity in terms of a measurement-conditioned posterior mean and showed that the ideal field transports the source distribution to the corresponding posterior. Across five restoration tasks on two datasets, our method achieves best overall distortion metrics at a fraction of the inference cost of flow-based solvers. Varying the number of sampling steps also allows a single trained model to span the distortion–perception trade-off without retraining. Limitations. Our theoretical analysis assumes a known linear forward model with additive Gaussian noise. Extending the framework to nonlinear measurement processes and more general noise models is an important direction for future work. We also focus on linear interpolation and explicit Euler sampling; investigating alternative probability paths and numerical solvers may further improve sampling efficiency. Finally, our experiments concentrate on two-dimensional image restoration, and applications to other imaging modalities remain to be explored.
